title: Skills without learning: Africa’s green industrialization “base” dilemma
body:
Across Africa, the conversation on green industrialization is saturated with one familiar concern: skills.

We hear the same message repeatedly—Africa needs more engineers. More technicians. More renewable energy specialists. It is thus unsurprising that across the continent, countries are investing in STEM education and green technology training.

This focus is understandable. Green industrialization in its full spectrum is technology-intensive, and building a skilled workforce matters. But skills alone do not create industrial transformation.

Consider two possible futures

- In the first, a country trains thousands of graduates in renewable energy and battery technologies. Yet domestic firms lack technological capabilities and production capacity. Solar panels, batteries, and wind turbines are imported.

The result? The country produces skilled graduates, but the industries that use those skills are located elsewhere. Graduates migrate. Some move into unrelated sectors. Ultimately green transition happens but largely without domestic industrialization.

- Now imagine a different scenario. Education investments are paired with industrial learning strategies. Governments support domestic firms entering renewable energy value chains. Local companies assemble solar components, experiment with battery recycling, and build electric mobility supply chains. Universities collaborate with industry.

The result? Skills do not sit idle. They are absorbed into a system that learns.

The latter reflects how industrial transformation historically occurred. From Japan to South Korea, skills expanded alongside industries that were actively learning by doing. Firms built capabilities through production. Workers developed tacit knowledge through experience. Institutions supported experimentation and technological adaptation.

Skills mattered because they were embedded in industrial ecosystems. Africa must follow a similar path if industrialization is the goal.

The real question is thus not simply: “How do we train more people?” It is: "What kind of economy will absorb and grow those skills?"

A learning economy is one where firms, workers, and institutions continuously experiment, adapt, and upgrade capabilities. Learning happens not only in universities, but in factories, workshops, supply chains, and industrial ecosystems.

**Bottom line:** Skills without learning = green transition without industrialization. If Africa wants to leverage green transition to drive real green industrialization, skills must be embedded in learning economies.

Africa’s green industrial future will not be built only in classrooms. It will be built in economies that learn. This requires shifting from human capital strategies to industrial learning strategies.
